identity.name: CIDOC-CRM
identity.originator: ICOM/CIDOC Documentation Standards Working Group, led by Martin Doerr (ICS-FORTH)
identity.key_text: Definition of the CIDOC Conceptual Reference Model, ISO 21127:2023

conceptual.core_claim: Cultural heritage information can be semantically integrated across institutions through a shared event-centric ontology that models objects, actors, places, and time-spans as participants in historical events.
conceptual.relation_to_attention_economy: Explicitly refuses attention logic. CIDOC-CRM serves institutional memory and scholarly inquiry, not engagement or discovery. Its temporality is archival and forensic, not real-time. However, its institutional adoption functions as a prestige signal within the museum-academic complex.
conceptual.relation_to_commons: [uncertain] Ambiguous. The ontology itself is an ISO standard (paywalled document) but the CRM definition is freely available on cidoc-crm.org. It is a commons in the sense of shared infrastructure, but governed by a small expert committee rather than an open community. Contributions require navigating institutional channels.
conceptual.epistemological_stance: Empirical-historical. Knowledge is valid when it can be traced to documented events with provenance. The model privileges what can be institutionally verified over what is emergent, contested, or frontier. Validity is determined by expert consensus within the CIDOC working group.

technical.architecture_pattern: Event-centric ontology graph. 81 classes and 160 properties organized around temporal entities (events) that connect persistent items (objects, people, places). Modular extensions (CRMsci, CRMdig, CRMarchaeo, LRMoo) specialize the core.
technical.data_model: RDF/OWL triples following the event-based pattern. Core relations include P14 (carried out by), P108 (has produced), P7 (took place at), P4 (has time-span). Every assertion is anchored to a production, modification, or transfer event.
technical.temporal_logic: Archival with chronological reasoning support (ISO 21127:2023 added temporal properties). Time is modeled as time-spans attached to events. Supports fuzzy dating through uncertain boundaries. No anticipatory or cyclical temporal logic.
technical.absence_handling: No native absence detection. The model represents what is known and documented. Gaps appear only as missing triples, with no mechanism to flag or diagnose structural absence. Lacunae are invisible unless a human researcher notices them.
technical.scalability_model: Centralized standard, federated implementation. Each institution maintains its own CRM-compliant dataset. Integration happens through semantic alignment at query time. The standard itself is centrally governed by the CIDOC CRM SIG.

garden_logic_comparative.layer_mapping: substrate — CIDOC-CRM operates at the data model layer, defining how cultural information is structured. It is infrastructure, not sensing or prompt-generation.
garden_logic_comparative.intention_vs_attention: Neither, strictly. CIDOC-CRM serves institutional documentation, not diagnosis or engagement. It does not optimize for intention (structural gap detection) because it cannot see what is missing. It does not optimize for attention because it has no discovery or ranking layer. It optimizes for archival fidelity — preserving what is known with maximal provenance. A(DAI) should note that archival fidelity is necessary but insufficient: the garden needs to sense what the archive cannot see.
garden_logic_comparative.coherence_vs_consensus: Strong consensus orientation. The ontology is developed through multi-year expert deliberation. Changes require formal proposals to the CRM SIG. This produces high semantic consistency but at the cost of responsiveness to frontier signals. Coherence (in A(DAI)'s sense of holding multiple valid readings simultaneously) is structurally impossible — the CRM resolves ambiguity toward canonical definitions.
garden_logic_comparative.contestability: Very low. The ontology's outputs are not designed to be contested by end users. Proposals for change go through the CRM SIG, which meets periodically. There is no mechanism for counter-signals, dissenting classifications, or parallel readings. The model assumes expert authority.
garden_logic_comparative.forkability: Technically forkable (the definition is published), but practically unforkable. A fork would break interoperability — the entire value proposition is institutional alignment on a single shared model. No provenance tracking across forks. The extension mechanism (CRMsci, CRMarchaeo) is the sanctioned alternative to forking.
garden_logic_comparative.tendency_axis_position: openness: semi-open (definition public, ISO document paywalled) | commons: institutional commons (shared but expert-governed) | spectacle: pure infrastructure | individual: distributed across institutions but governed centrally
garden_logic_comparative.what_adai_should_adopt: The event-centric data model pattern. Anchoring assertions to events (creation, exhibition, collaboration, critique) rather than static attributes gives A(DAI)'s graph temporal depth and forensic traceability. The typed relationship vocabulary (P14 carried out by, P108 has produced) is a proven pattern for the kind of dense edge networks A(DAI) needs. The modular extension architecture shows how a core ontology can specialize without breaking.
garden_logic_comparative.what_adai_should_refuse: The consensus governance model. A(DAI) must refuse the assumption that ontological authority flows from expert committees. The CRM's inability to accommodate frontier signals — things that don't yet have institutional names — is exactly the gap A(DAI) exists to fill. Also refuse: the assumption that ambiguity should be resolved rather than held. A(DAI)'s coherence model requires that contested edges remain visible, not collapsed into canonical readings.
garden_logic_comparative.structural_tension: The deepest tension is between interoperability and frontier sensitivity. CIDOC-CRM achieves interoperability precisely by fixing categories. A(DAI) achieves frontier sensitivity precisely by keeping categories fluid. If A(DAI) ever needs to export data to institutional systems, it will face a lossy translation at the CRM boundary — frontier signals and contested edges have no CRM equivalent. This tension is productive: it forces A(DAI) to design explicit translation layers rather than assuming ontological universality.

critical.limits: Extremely high adoption cost. Requires deep ontological expertise to model data correctly. The event-centric pattern, while powerful, creates verbose graphs for simple assertions. 81 classes and 160 properties create a steep learning curve. Extensions add further complexity. The model assumes institutional data practices that many smaller organizations and independent practitioners cannot sustain.
critical.who_is_excluded: [uncertain] Independent practitioners, self-taught artists, frontier practices without institutional documentation, oral traditions not captured in provenance records, non-Western knowledge organization systems that don't map to the event-centric Western archival model. Anyone whose practice has not been documented by an institution is structurally invisible.
critical.failure_under_attention: [uncertain] If the attention economy leaks in, CIDOC-CRM becomes a prestige credentialing system — institutions that adopt it gain legitimacy over those that don't. The ontology's authority becomes a gatekeeping mechanism rather than an interoperability tool. LLM-driven auto-classification (the 2025 GPT-based triple extraction research) could accelerate this by making CRM-compliance a checkbox for AI-readiness, regardless of whether the model actually serves the collection.

governance.governance_model: Expert committee within an international standards body (ICOM/CIDOC). Changes proposed through formal SIG meetings. ISO standardization adds a further governance layer with national body voting.
governance.consent_architecture: [uncertain] Implicit consent through adoption. Institutions choose to adopt the standard; there is no mechanism for individuals whose work is described by the standard to consent to or contest their representation. No machine-readable consent layer.

materiality.extraction_vector: [uncertain] Extracts expert labor (ontological modeling requires specialized knowledge). Does not directly extract from artists or practitioners, but creates a representation layer they cannot control or contest. The ISO standardization process extracts institutional subscription fees.
materiality.composability: Modular via extension mechanism (CRMsci, CRMdig, etc.). Can be embedded in larger systems. RDF/OWL foundation allows interoperability with other semantic web vocabularies. Not API-first but protocol-level (RDF is the protocol).
materiality.liveness: Actively maintained. ISO 21127:2023 is the latest edition. CRM SIG meets regularly. Summer School 2025 held. Over 400 projects worldwide. Living standard with institutional momentum.
materiality.scale_of_operation: Institutional to field-level. Designed for museums, archives, libraries. Cross-institutional integration is the primary use case. Not designed for individual-scale or small-group use.
materiality.temporality: Deep historical depth. Designed to model events spanning millennia. Chronological reasoning added in 2023 edition. No cyclical, anticipatory, or tidal temporal logic. Time is linear and archival.
